title: Cook's Second Voyage: The Resolution and the Adventure
intro: James Cook sailed in the Resolution, with the Adventure under Tobias Furneaux, on a voyage commissioned by the British government with advice from the Royal Society. It was designed to circumnavigate the globe as far south as possible and to settle whether a great southern landmass, Terra Australis, existed.
ending: The Resolution anchored at Spithead on 30 July 1775. Cook's reports put to rest the myth of Terra Australis, and the Larcum Kendall K1 chronometer had let him fix his longitude with much greater accuracy.

legs.title: To the Cape and round to New Zealand

stops.text: The Resolution and the Adventure left Plymouth Sound on a Monday. The Resolution carried a crew of 112, among them the astronomer William Wales, the artist William Hodges and the Royal Society scientists Johann Reinhold Forster and his son Georg.
stops.quote: Cook's second voyage of discovery departed Plymouth Sound on Monday 13 July 1772.

stops.text: The first port of call was Funchal in the Madeira Islands. From Funchal Roads Cook reported to the Admiralty on the sailing qualities of the Resolution before sailing on after a short stay.
stops.quote: His first port of call was at Funchal in the Madeira Islands, which he reached on 1 August.

stops.text: The ships took on water at Porto Praya on San Tiago, in the Cape Verde Islands. Cook and Wales surveyed the bay, the Forsters collected plants, and hogs, goats, poultry and fruit were plentiful.
stops.quote: After a short stay, Cook sailed for Porto Praya, San Tiago (Cape Verde Islands), arriving at 12 August.

stops.text: Both ships anchored near Cape Town. The Swedish naturalist Anders Sparrman joined the expedition there as an assistant naturalist at his own expense, and Wales and Bayly checked the chronometers.
stops.quote: On 30 October, both ships anchored in Table Bay near Capetown.

stops.text: After the Antarctic Circle was first crossed on 17 January 1773 and the ships were separated in fog on 8 February, the Resolution sighted New Zealand and Cook entered Dusky Sound. The crew recovered with fresh water, wood and fish, and met cautious but curious Māori.
stops.quote: Cook risked entering Dusky Sound on the South Island to find shelter and resources after a long and difficult voyage.

stops.text: The Resolution anchored in Ship Cove, in Queen Charlotte Sound, and was rejoined by the Adventure, which had arrived on 7 April. Cook planned to use the winter to explore the uncharted seas to the east and north.
stops.quote: The Resolution dropped anchor in Ship Cove, and Captain Furneaux of the Adventure came aboard.

legs.title: The Pacific in the southern winter and spring

stops.text: Both ships reached Tahiti and stopped at Vaitepiha Bay so that the Adventure's sick could go ashore for fresh food and rest. Tahiti had recently been through a civil war, and the hog breeding Cook relied on had been disrupted. Cook left Tautira on 24 August.
stops.quote: Cook decided to leave Tautira on 24 August.

stops.text: Cook met the chief Maritata, who promised to introduce him to Prince Otoo. Cook and Furneaux visited Otoo the next day, and Omai joined the Adventure and Porio the Resolution when the ships left.
stops.quote: At Matavai Bay on 26 August, Cook met chief Maritata, who promised to introduce him to Prince Otoo.

stops.text: The chief Ori, who had hosted Cook before, welcomed the ships, and hogs were bought in numbers. Sparrman, collecting plants alone, was attacked by two local men who stripped him of his clothes and knife and chased him along the beach.
stops.quote: On 3 September, both ships set sail for Huahine and Raiatea.

stops.text: The people of Tongatapu welcomed the visitors and brought out canoes of provisions. After thefts, Cook ordered muskets fired at one man and others tied up and flogged. He later called Eua, Tongatapu and Nomuka the Friendly Archipelago.
stops.quote: On 8 October Cook set sail bound for New Zealand. After leaving Tongatapu, Cook faced immediate difficulties at sea.

stops.text: The Resolution reached Queen Charlotte Sound after a gale off Cook Strait, but the Adventure, parted from her on 30 October, was not there. Cook left a message buried under a marked tree and sailed on 25 November.
stops.quote: made his way to Ship Cove in Queen Charlotte Sound, arriving on 3 November

stops.text: Furneaux's cutter, sent for greens, did not return. Burney's search party found shoes, a hand identified as Thomas Hill's and dismembered bodies at Grass Cove, and fired on the Māori there.
stops.quote: In Grass Cove, upon arrival, the English encountered four canoes and a crowd of Native people who quickly retreated to a nearby hill.

legs.title: The second Antarctic crossing and the islands of the south-west Pacific

stops.text: After crossing the Antarctic Circle for the third time on 26 January and turning back from the ice at 71° S, the Resolution sighted Easter Island. Cook recognised it by its location and the moai, and Cook himself had been dangerously ill.
stops.quote: On 11 March 1774, after three months without sighting land, the Resolution finally saw a small island on the horizon.

stops.text: Cook sailed for the port Mendaña had used in the Marquesas, on Tahuata. Canoes came out to trade, but theft by islanders brought a violent response from the crew, and a local man died. Trade resumed later.
stops.quote: Cook aimed for Mendafia's port, now known as Vaitahu Bay on Tahuata. Canoes approached to trade, but theft by islanders led to a violent response from the crew, resulting in a local man's death.

stops.text: The Resolution anchored in Tahiti after passing through the Tuamotu atolls. The crew's scurvy had gone, supplies were restocked and Wales checked the chronometer.
stops.quote: After discovering more atolls, named Palliser's Isles, he reached Tahiti and anchored in Matavai Bay on 22 April.

stops.text: The English met hostility and theft, and Cook used force to recover stolen goods. Relations then improved and regular trade began. Cook declined the offer of a young woman, which upset her family.
stops.quote: At Nomuka, the English faced initial hostility and theft, prompting Cook to use force to recover stolen items.

stops.text: In the New Hebrides, a conflict broke out during an attempted landing at Eromanga, with injuries on both sides. The English found the Eromangans different from the Malekulans in appearance and language.
stops.quote: At Eromanga, a conflict broke out during an attempted landing, resulting in injuries on both sides.

stops.text: An active volcano drew scientific interest. The English met resistance at first, then traded. Islanders blocked them from parts of the island, which they later realised were sacred. They stayed more than two weeks.
stops.quote: Next, the Resolution visited Tanna, where an active volcano drew scientific interest.

stops.text: The Resolution reached New Caledonia, and Cook gave the island that name. The English noted that the tall, strong islanders were open with them and that there was no theft.
stops.quote: After leaving the New Hebrides, the Resolution discovered New Caledonia, where the people impressed the English with their openness and honesty despite limited resources.

stops.text: The Resolution sighted the Isle of Pines and Norfolk Island, both valued for their timber, then returned to New Zealand. There the Māori assured Cook that all was well, though the Adventure had gone.
stops.quote: discovering the Isle of Pines and Norfolk Island, valued for their timber.

legs.title: Homeward by Cape Horn and the Atlantic

stops.text: After rounding Cape Horn at the end of December 1774, the Resolution sighted land in icy conditions: no continent, but an island of seals, penguins and birds, which Johann Forster named South Georgia. The ship left on 20 January 1775.
stops.quote: Later, the crew sighted land in icy conditions and found not a continent, but an inhospitable island, named South Georgia by J. R. Forster.

stops.text: The Resolution anchored for repairs after a long voyage, and Sparrman left to continue his botanical studies. At sea Cook had heard from passing ships that Furneaux's crew had suffered casualties in New Zealand.
stops.quote: By late March, the Resolution anchored at Cape Town for repairs.

stops.text: After five weeks of repairs the Resolution sailed with the Dutton to St Helena, where Cook met an old acquaintance, John Skottowe, and wrote a favourable account of the island.
stops.quote: arrived at St Helena, where Cook met an old acquaintance, John Skottowe.

stops.text: The Resolution anchored at Spithead, ending more than three years of exploration. Cook was promoted to captain and made a Fellow of the Royal Society.
stops.quote: The voyage ended on 30 July 1775, when the Resolution anchored at Spithead, concluding over three years of exploration.

notes: Grass Cove: the article gives no day for Burney's search; the stop is the Adventure's, placed after the Resolution's 3 November Ship Cove stop (Grass Cove lies in Queen Charlotte Sound). wp is given as Ship Cove because Grass Cove may lack its own article; the editor may supply a better title or point. The quote is the Adventure's arrival there. The article calls the Māori 'Native people' in that passage and does not say why the cutter's crew were killed. Years for Tautira, Matavai Bay 1773, Huahine, Tongatapu, Dusky Sound and the 1774 Vanuatu and New Caledonia stops are inferred from the surrounding narrative; the article gives no year or day there. Dusky Sound: article gives no date; the article puts the first Antarctic crossing on 17 January 1773 and the separation on 8 February. Eromanga: wp Erromango. Left out: Antarctic Circle crossings (not places), Cape Horn (no event), Tasmania (Adventure only), Raiatea, Eua, Malekula, Cape Palliser, Ascension Island. The article says Cook 'discovered' New Caledonia in the quote; text says reached.
